justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price near 1000, with the trajectory staying relatively flat across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the 1005 estimate essentially assumes mean-reverting, low-volatility conditions with a slight positive bias, consistent with markets that are not under immediate stress. At one week, the 1010 estimate incorporates a small additional drift premium, acknowledging that over slightly longer windows, asset prices in non-crisis environments tend to grind modestly higher on average. At one month, the 1020 estimate continues that gentle upward slope, though the incremental gain is modest because I did not assume any strong fundamental catalyst driving a sharp directional move. In all cases, the point estimates are closer to "more of the same" than to any dramatic repricing.

The confidence interval widths expand in a fairly standard way as the horizon lengthens, reflecting the well-established principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 60-point range around the estimate reflects normal intraday-to-overnight volatility. At one week, the 110-point range accounts for the possibility of a macro data release, central bank communication, or geopolitical headline that could shift sentiment meaningfully in either direction. At one month, the 200-point range reflects all of those shorter-term risks plus the cumulative possibility of a regime shift in market conditions, earnings surprises, or a sustained change in rate expectations. The widths are moderate rather than extreme because I assumed no obviously imminent high-impact event at the time of forecasting.

The most significant risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals fall into a few broad categories. A sudden liquidity event, a surprise central bank action, or a geopolitical shock could easily push prices 5–10% beyond the outer bounds of my one-week or one-month intervals. On the upside, a strong coordinated risk-on move driven by better-than-expected economic data or a resolution of a known geopolitical risk could cause a rally that exceeds my upper bounds. On the downside, a credit event, a flash crash dynamic, or an unexpected policy reversal could cause a drawdown beyond the lower bounds. My intervals implicitly assume a relatively benign, continuous-price environment, and any discontinuous jump process — a gap open, a circuit-breaker event — would invalidate the assumptions baked into those ranges.
